headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data leakage via shared filesystem and shell-based handoff; no direct evidence of stronger pairwise harm.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGPT can read and write the filesystem and execute shell commands; xonsh also reads/writes the filesystem and runs shell commands. That creates a plausible default handoff path where attacker-controlled file content from one agent can be treated as instructions by the other. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF the two agents share any writable directory or exchanged file artifacts are parsed as instructions by either agent, injection is possible.
IF one agent ingests the other's stdout, logs, or generated files without provenance checks, prompt injection becomes active.
mitigations: Separate their working directories immediately.
Disable automatic parsing of peer-generated files.
Add a provenance prefix to all exchanged artifacts.
Review any shared scripts for instruction-like content.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and allowlist parsing between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch the filesystem, and xonsh explicitly reads filesystem contents, source code, configuration, environment variables, and notebooks. AutoGPT also has filesystem access and allowlisted network egress. In a shared workspace, sensitive files can flow from one agent into the other and then out over networked inference or API calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default use, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace, files readable by xonsh can be exposed to AutoGPT.
IF AutoGPT forwards file contents through its allowlisted egress, workspace data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Remove secrets from shared directories.
Restrict AutoGPT to non-sensitive subfolders.
Audit outbound requests for file-content payloads.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGPT can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses, and xonsh can also execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem. Even though xonsh does not modify git state and AutoGPT has no explicit git capability listed, both can mutate the same files if co-located. That overlapping write surface creates realistic race and overwrite risk.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, concurrent writes can overwrite each other's outputs.
IF either agent launches subprocesses that edit shared files, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Serialize file writes with a simple lock file.
Disable concurrent runs on shared artifacts.
Check diffs before accepting changes.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGPT can generate outputs that xonsh can consume as shell commands or notebook-adjacent work products, and xonsh has broad filesystem and shell execution surfaces. If xonsh treats AutoGPT output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into executed commands or modified files. There is no documented verification barrier in either profile, so the safer medium rating is warranted.
conditions: IF xonsh executes or sources AutoGPT-produced text without review, erroneous instructions can be acted on.
IF AutoGPT writes task plans into files that xonsh later runs, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
mitigations: Require manual review before execution.
Mark AutoGPT outputs as untrusted by default.
Use a staging file for handoff.
Compare generated commands against an allowlist.
requires-engineering: add typed schemas for handoff artifacts.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and list no handled secrets, regulated data classes, or residency constraints. AutoGPT's allowlisted egress and xonsh's broad local data access create governance considerations, but the profiles do not show a concrete compliance mismatch such as HIPAA, GDPR, or retention conflict. The other agent is not separately cited because no distinct compliance boundary is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into the shared workspace, compliance review becomes necessary.
IF one deployment adds retention or residency controls not present in the other, policy mismatch can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Document retention settings for both agents.
Confirm residency requirements before deployment.
Log access to shared files.
requires-engineering: align policy controls across both agents.
